objectives.text: Without references, DISCUSS the hazards associated with chemicals (liquid and gas) found in a nuclear plant.

enabling.text: STATE the hazards associated with the use of corrosives.
STATE the general safety precautions necessary for the handling, storage, and disposal of corrosives.
LIST the general safety precautions regarding toxic compounds.
LIST the criteria used to determine if a compound is a health hazard.
STATE the methods by which toxic compounds may enter the body.
SUMMARIZE the purpose and general contents of the following:
STATE the five major families of gases.
STATE the general safety precautions regarding the use, handling, and storage of gases.
STATE the safety precautions for working with cryogenic liquids.

LIST four sources of ignition of flammable liquids.
STATE the health hazards associated with flammable and/or combustible liquids.

checks.q: Why are alkalies more injurious to the eyes than acids?
o: Strong acids precipitate a protein barrier, and alkalies do not
checks.x: Strong acids tend to precipitate a protein barrier. Alkalies continue to soak into the tissue.

checks.q: What gas do acids liberate when they react with many metals?
checks.x: Acids react with many metals, liberating hydrogen, a highly flammable gas.

checks.q: Why must cold water be used to dissolve solid alkalies?
o: Much heat is evolved, and the solution may boil and splatter
checks.x: Much heat is evolved, so with warmer water the solution may boil and splatter corrosive liquid.

checks.q: By which methods can toxic compounds enter the body?
checks.x: Industrial poisonings usually result from inhalation, ingestion, and absorption.

checks.q: How does hazard differ from toxicity?
o: Hazard is the possibility of injury under specific conditions of use
checks.x: Toxicity is the capacity to harm. Hazard is the possibility of injury with a specific quantity under specific conditions.

concepts.title: MSDS and the Toxic Substances List

body.text: The MSDS identifies the chemical by technical and common name, and lists physical and chemical characteristics and fire, explosion, and reactivity hazards.
It also specifies health hazards, first aid procedures, and safe handling and control measures.
Absence from the list does not necessarily mean a substance is not toxic.

checks.q: What is the purpose of a Material Safety Data Sheet?
o: To give specific information on chemicals to the people working with them
To list all known toxic substances
checks.x: The MSDS ensures that individuals working with chemicals have specific information on them.

checks.q: What does listing a substance on the Toxic Substances List mean?
o: It has the documented potential of being hazardous if misused
checks.x: Presence on the list does not mean avoid it. It means it has documented potential to be hazardous if misused.

body.text: A compressed gas gives a pressure reading of either 25 psig at 70 °F or 125 psig at 130 °F, or if flammable, 25 psig at 100 °F.
Acetylene is sometimes referred to as a dissolved gas.

checks.q: Which is one of the five major families of gases?
checks.x: The families are atmospheric, fuel, refrigerant, aerosol, and poison gases.

checks.q: What is a dissolved gas?
o: A gas that is dissolved into a solution
A gas that liquifies in its container
checks.x: A dissolved gas is defined as a gas that is dissolved into a solution.

body.text: The chief precaution is adequate ventilation of enclosed areas. Do not enter unventilated areas without breathing apparatus.
Oxygen should be stored no closer than 10 feet to cylinders or tanks containing flammable gases.
Cylinders should be chained so they cannot fall, and a broken valve could make a cylinder a projectile.
Cryogenic liquids and their boil-off vapor can rapidly freeze human tissue and make materials brittle.
Vaporized in a sealed container, they produce enormous pressures, so containers usually have two pressure-relief devices.
Stand clear of boiling or splashing liquid, and never let an unprotected body part touch uninsulated pipes or vessels.

checks.q: What is the chief precaution against gases acting as asphyxiants?
checks.x: Practically all gases can displace oxygen, and the chief precaution is adequate ventilation.

checks.q: Why should gloves for cryogenic work be loose fitting?
o: So they can be removed quickly if liquids are spilled into them
checks.x: Gloves should be loose fitting so they can be removed quickly if liquids are spilled into them.

checks.q: How should gas cylinders be moved?
checks.x: Cylinders should not be dragged or rolled across the floor. They should be moved by a hand truck.

body.text: Hydrogen is the lightest of all elements and cannot be detected by any of the senses.
Precautions include adequate ventilation and eliminating possible sources of ignition. Hydrogen is classified as an asphyxiant.
Nitrogen makes up more than 78 percent of the atmosphere, and it is frequently used to inert systems.
Oxygen should never be used to run pneumatic equipment, and it should always be called oxygen, not air.

checks.q: What is the flammable range of hydrogen in air, by volume?
checks.x: Hydrogen has a flammable range of from 4.1 percent to 74.2 percent by volume in air.

checks.q: What happens when metallic sodium is exposed to water?
o: It reacts violently, producing hydrogen that may flame spontaneously
checks.x: Metallic sodium reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen, which may flame spontaneously.

checks.q: What may happen when oxygen contacts oil or grease?
checks.x: When oxygen comes in contact with oil, grease, or fuel oils, it may ignite violently.

checks.q: What is the hazard of a large nitrogen release into an enclosed space?
checks.x: A large release could cause a serious oxygen deficiency. Nitrogen is an asphyxiant.

body.text: Fire needs three factors in the right quantity at one place and time.
To prevent a fire, keep one of these factors away from the other two.

items: Improper type of electrical equipment, or poorly maintained electrical equipment
Flame-producing operations such as smoking, grinding, or welding
Improper hand tools that cause sparks

checks.q: What three factors are needed for a fire?
checks.x: The factors are fuel, heat, and oxygen.

checks.q: What separates a flammable liquid from a combustible liquid?
checks.x: A flammable liquid has a flash point below 100 °F, and a combustible liquid at or above 100 °F but below 200 °F.

checks.q: When should a combustible liquid be treated as flammable?
checks.x: Combustible liquids should be treated as flammable when they are heated.

steps: Absolute pressure is atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi) plus gauge pressure

facts.q: How long should eyes be irrigated after contact with a corrosive?
facts.a: With water for at least 15 minutes, and a physician should be consulted immediately.

facts.q: How do acute and chronic poisoning differ?
facts.a: Acute is rapid absorption from sudden, severe exposure. Chronic is absorption of small doses over a long period of time.

facts.q: What does oxygen do to combustion?
facts.a: It does not burn, but it lowers the ignition point of flammable substances and greatly accelerates combustion.

facts.q: How much do cryogenic liquids expand on vaporizing?
facts.a: They produce large volumes of gas. One volume of liquid nitrogen vaporizes to 696.5 volumes of gas at room temperature.
The minimum temperature at which a liquid gives off vapor in sufficient concentration to form an ignitible mixture with air near its surface.

summary.text: Acids can destroy body tissue, and alkalies are more destructive than the acids.
Toxic compounds may enter the body by ingestion, inhalation, and absorption.
The major families of gases are atmospheric, fuel, refrigerant, aerosol, and poison gases.
Hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen each need their own precautions.
Bonding eliminates a difference in potential between objects, and grounding between an object and ground.
